Talos treats the swarm as unintended rather than malicious, but a Tencent-hosted agent fleet and the ARTEX framework have since adopted the same tricks. articles.headline: Bring Your Own Interpreter - EDR Evasion with LuaJIT, Julia, Node.js, Deno, and Bun
articles.blurb: Trusted, signed interpreters like LuaJIT, Julia, Node.js, Deno, and Bun can use their built-in FFI to allocate RWX memory with VirtualAllocExNuma, copy in shellcode, and pass that buffer as the callback to EnumUILanguagesW. Windows itself then calls the shellcode, so there's no injection API, no PE on disk, and no direct jump for an EDR to flag. The researcher's calc.exe proof of concept got past ESET, but the earlier Elastic, Defender for Endpoint, and Sophos results come from older tests of similar code. Defenders should block unapproved runtimes with WDAC or AppLocker outside developer machines and alert when interpreter processes allocate executable memory or call Win32 APIs through FFI.

Each patch is built from the exact Proxmox kernel source, tested in QEMU, and signed, then checked against signature, build-id, and hash before it loads, with canary, early, and stable release rings, automatic rollback, and an option to self-host the pipeline with your own keys. It's still early-release software, with the 7.0 kernel experimental and no bare-metal soak yet, and changes to data structures and ZFS fixes still need a reboot, but status shows clearly which CVEs are fixed live and which aren't.

Its planner agent works from a knowledge graph and hands short attack "intents" to worker agents running nmap, sqlmap, hydra, and Metasploit, which can take an intrusion from reconnaissance to privileged access in minutes using any LLM, including models with their guardrails stripped. Microsoft notes that ARTEX introduces no new techniques and that operators routinely change IPs and user agents, so the most durable signal is its machine-speed pattern of bursts and retries, while ThreatBook's claim of ownership and its commercial "ARTEX Pro" add a new twist to the tool's spread.
